As a demonstration of this theoretical framework, we demonstrate that the Hausdorff dimension of a compact subspace $K$ contained within a self-similar fractal $X$ adheres to the following bound:
$$\dim_{H}(K)\leqslant\dim_{H}(X)-\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\dim_{H}(H_{j}),$$
where $\dim_{H}(.)$ denotes the Hausdorff dimension, and $\{H_{j}\}$ represents a sequence of compact subspaces of $X$ derived from the homology groups of $K$. The primary focus of this research is the extension of the Euler characteristic to fractal geometry. This generalization is achieved by defining the ($\dim_{H}$-based) fractal dimension of the extended Euler characteristic through a power-law relationship. Consequently, this approach yields novel characterizations of compact sets within fractal geometries. Furthermore, the study establishes that the homology functor is non-increasing with respect to the partial order of compact subspaces under the subset relation, and the inverse image functor is non-decreasing with respect to the partial order of extended Euler characteristic under the order relation. Finally, the dimension and the (non-inverted) inverse image functor are characterized using these established properties. These findings offer new perspectives on the application of the Euler characteristic in topology and homology theory. Furthermore, the study provides a new characterization for the Hausdorff dimension of compact sets in self-similar geometries, along with a generalization of the post-critically finite (PCF) condition in homology theory. This work serves as a foundational step toward characterizing the inverse image functor in a broader context. Additionally, the dimension of the inverse image functor is computed to demonstrate the validity of this foundational step. The results are applied to the Cantor set, the Sierpinski gasket, and the Menger sponge to illustrate the utility of the proposed methodology. These applications reveal that the inverse image functor exhibits non-trivial behavior in these well-known fractal spaces, thereby providing a foundation for future research. The research also offers an alternative method for calculating the Hausdorff dimension of generalized spaces, such as generalized Cantor sets, generalized Sierpinski gaskets, and generalized Menger spaces. This paper introduces a family of such Hirsch counterexamples in higher dimensions. Our findings indicate that EVBA yields a reliable estimate of the differential cross section in the forward region, where vector boson rapidity separations ($|\Delta y_{W,Z}|$) are large and jet pseudorapidities ($\eta_{jet}$) are extreme. However, in the central region, a substantial correction term is required. We determine that this correction is well-modeled by a term proportional to $\frac{M_H^2}{s}$ scaled by a factor of order unity. This leading correction arises from interference effects between the full theory and the vector boson approximation, as well as between different vector boson channels. We provide an explicit formula for the correction applied to EVBA cross sections and validate these results through next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD calculations using the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO software. Finally, we discuss the implications of these corrections for measuring the Higgs coupling to electroweak gauge bosons. Given that the correction is primarily driven by interference between vector boson production and standard model background processes, it does not influence the electroweak production cross section at the $\mathcal{O}(v^2)$ level. Consequently, the corrected VBF differential cross section can be directly utilized to measure the $hh$ production cross section via VBF. Furthermore, under the standard model hypothesis, this method offers a model-independent way to extract the electroweak coupling $\kappa_{ZHH}$ from the differential cross section. We conclude that the proposed method is more effective than the standard VBF strategy for these measurements. Additionally, we demonstrate that the VBF method outperforms diphoton decay channel methods in measuring $\kappa_Z$. We also examine the utility of the extracted cross section for probing anomalous electroweak couplings. Finally, we address the potential for measuring the time-reversal violating phase in the $ZZHH$ vertex using the extracted cross section. This approach is applicable to the high-luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and future colliders. We further illustrate how to incorporate the extracted cross section into the likelihood function for the purpose of measuring the electroweak coupling. In summary, the methodology presented in this paper offers a more precise and sensitive tool for determining the electroweak coupling compared to existing methods. We anticipate that the techniques

To address this, knowledge distillation has been introduced as a strategy to accelerate policy learning by enabling agents to acquire policies from pre-trained ones. However, this standard approach is ill-suited for RL because the original policy is typically not explicitly available. Consequently, this paper proposes a new RL framework that learns policies from the behavioral patterns of pre-trained agents. To overcome the challenge of extracting policies from implicit state values, we present a latent action space construction method that decomposes actions into a continuous component and a discrete component. Furthermore, to mitigate training difficulties caused by a mismatch between teacher and student action spaces, we present a curriculum learning framework that gradually transitions from the teacher's action space to the student's. Experimental evaluations across three distinct RL tasks demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully and efficiently extracts policies from the pre-trained behaviors. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for future research aimed at streamlining policy learning from pre-trained agents. 17-BLG-1410 was observed by the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) and the Chilean Astronomical Society (CASLE). By combining the OGLE and CASLE datasets, we identified a planet with a mass of $0.01\,\mathrm{M_J}$ orbiting a host star every $1.7$ years. This host star is likely a brown dwarf, given its high mass and the planet's proximity. The system's architecture resembles a scaled-down version of OGLE-2016-BLG-1098, featuring a massive host and a close, low-mass planetary companion. This observation supports the hypothesis that the frequency of massive substellar hosts increases as the planet mass decreases. Additionally, the planet's high mass relative to its orbital period suggests it formed via core accretion. The detection of such a massive, close-in planet around a brown dwarf aligns with the core accretion model's prediction that massive planets form more readily around massive objects. This finding further strengthens the core accretion theory, which is supported by numerous substellar hosts and massive planets in close orbits. The identification of OGLE-2017-BLG-1410 as a brown dwarf host significantly expands the population of known substellar objects. Furthermore, the system's high signal-to-noise ratio and the host's brown dwarf nature make it an ideal candidate for future direct imaging and spectroscopic analysis. Finally, OGLE-2017-BLG-1410 is the first brown dwarf host identified using the OGLE survey. The collaboration between OGLE and CASLE has proven effective in detecting and characterizing exoplanetary systems, and this partnership is expected to yield more such discoveries. This system may also serve as a valuable benchmark for upcoming wide-field microlensing surveys. In conclusion, OGLE-2017-BLG-1410 is a notable new exoplanetary system that enhances our understanding of substellar objects and their surrounding environments. The discovery of a massive planet in a close orbit around a brown dwarf in this system underscores the core accretion theory's ability to explain the formation of massive planets around substellar objects. The identification of OGLE-2017-BLG-1410 as the first brown dwarf host discovered by the OGLE survey marks a significant milestone in exoplanet research. disappearance of the B850 exciton band in chiral liquid crystalline films of self-assembled $\beta$-carotene microcrystals when subjected to a 0.3 T magnetic field at room temperature. These findings are interpreted as evidence of magnetic field-induced long-range order within the chiral $\beta$-carotene molecules. Additionally, the paper outlines a theoretical framework for exciton formation under such conditions. This model posits that the $\beta$-carotene chiral molecules organize into helical, long-range ordered domains, with the specific helicity determined by the applied magnetic field. Supported by Monte Carlo simulations, the results indicate that neutron depolarization data aligns with a mean-field long-range order of chiral molecules, characterized by a field-dependent critical magnetic field and a corresponding critical temperature. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the broadening of the B850 band is a direct consequence of the chiral molecular arrangement. Finally, the study confirms that exciton formation in $\beta$-carotene occurs exclusively within the chiral R50 band, which remains unaffected by the magnetic field. These outcomes provide a robust explanation for neutron depolarization measurements across various chiral systems and offer a novel approach to investigating long-range order in liquid crystalline films composed of self-assembled microcrystals. The proposed mechanism is also applicable to other chiral liquid crystalline films, including those made of cellulose. Furthermore, this mechanism offers a fresh perspective on the origin of biological homochirality. In this context, the $\beta$-carotene long-range order observed in this work suggests that the energy required to reverse chirality is significantly lower than previously assumed, a factor that could have been overcome by external energy sources during the emergence of life. This study presents a pilot survey of the HI distribution within the Coma cluster's outskirts, utilizing the Nancay Radiotelescope (NRT) alongside the Paris Observatory's 11.5m and 15m telescopes. The survey covers a 1.5-degree field of view with a velocity resolution of 1 km/s. By combining these instruments, we achieve a total sensitivity of 0.02 Jy/beam, enabling the detection of diffuse HI with surface brightness as low as 10 mJy/beam. We identified 12 cluster HI clouds, including two previously unknown, low-brightness clouds. These detections are consistent with theoretical models predicting diffuse gas in cluster surroundings. Additionally, we identified 11 known galaxies, with 10 exhibiting HI column densities exceeding the sensitivity limit. We detected extended HI envelopes around NGC 4889 and NGC 4535, with column densities ranging from 10^20 to 10^21 cm^-2. The HI distribution in the Coma cluster outskirts is characterized by a complex structure featuring both discrete and diffuse clouds. This survey successfully identified known HI-rich galaxies and diffuse gas, demonstrating that such observations can constrain models regarding the formation and evolution of galaxies and the cosmic web. Furthermore, the pilot survey's success suggests that a future NRT survey of the Coma cluster's outer regions is viable, provided the telescope's tracking system is upgraded. These results also underscore the value of using small telescopes for small-field surveys. We conclude that a future NRT survey of the Coma cluster's outskirts, utilizing a 100% duty cycle and a 1 km/s velocity resolution, could detect diffuse HI with a surface brightness of 10 mJy/beam. This approach would cover a 2.5-degree field of view over a 1000 km/s radial distance, resulting in a sensitivity of 0.04 Jy/beam. Such an observation would provide a substantial enhancement in sensitivity and velocity resolution compared to current surveys, thereby significantly improving our understanding of the cosmic web's morphology and evolution. The proposed survey is estimated to cost 100,000 EUR. We also outline the scientific case for this survey and the associated technical requirements for NRT. Finally, we present a proof of concept by simulating the projected survey's sensitivity

We demonstrate that this robustness can be enhanced by incorporating a regularization term into the loss function, where the specific form of this term is governed by the concept of topological richness. Topological richness quantifies the complexity of a network's output surface based on its homological properties and is effectively measured using persistent homology. Our approach involves augmenting the loss function of standard training methods with a regulation term derived from the homological features of network outputs. This paper introduces a novel consensus approach for TPC-Distributed Databases (TPC-DB) that integrates the Paxos algorithm with the two-phase commit (2PC) protocol. We introduce the concept of "Paxos-2PC," where the GetZPC phase of 2PC functions as an Outer Decider, and the Prepare/Accept phases are streamlined to accommodate transactions. By leveraging the fact that most transactions involve only a minimal number of rows, Paxos reduces the number of rounds in 2PC, thereby enhancing transaction performance. Furthermore, we present an optimization strategy for handling read-only transactions, which bypasses the 2PC protocol entirely and directly accesses the stable storage of all replicas. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms both the Narwhal algorithm and the traditional TPC-Distributed Database protocol. Additionally, we develop a new simulation environment for TPC-DB that supports the co-location of multiple TPC-DB transactions. This environment facilitates the testing and evaluation of novel TPC-DB transaction processing techniques. Our implementation of this approach has been successfully deployed in the TPC-Distributed Database v6.01, the latest version of the TPC-Distributed Database benchmark. The primary objective of this work is to investigate the microscopical behavior of the universe at the quantum level. We find that $\lambda$ is determined by the quantum state of gravitational energy, which is estimated to be near the Planck scale. This result is consistent with the expectation that microphysical processes occur at the quantum level. Consequently, the parameter $\lambda$ is comparable to the Planck length and significantly smaller than the observable universe's scale. In conclusion, our findings support the hypothesis that the microphysical behavior of the universe is governed by quantum mechanics. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. We argue, however, that the quantum state of the system does not allow for the unambiguous identification of the specific configuration the particles might be in. Furthermore, we contend that the quantum states representing the three particles are not orthogonal, meaning the particles cannot be said to have no interaction. Additionally, we present a method to prepare a state corresponding to a specific configuration, allowing us to measure the probability of that configuration occurring. Our results indicate that no configuration is preferred, though it is possible to make the most probable configuration more likely. Finally, we note that the term "interferometric arrangement" is somewhat misleading, as the setup is not merely an apparatus for observing interference, but also includes a source of particles and a way to direct them into the boxes. In this context, the term "quantum" is also somewhat redundant. Overall, we conclude that the effect is not as clear-cut as previously suggested. In a separate discussion, we explore the quantum states of the three particles in this setup, which are entangled across all three particles. We show that these states can be expressed as a superposition of the GHZ state and the W state, both of which are maximally robust entangled states. We also discuss the quantum states of the particles and their relationships from the perspective of entanglement witnesses. We observe that the quantum state of the system remains robust against white noise, and we propose a method to quantify this robustness using the relative entropy of entanglement. We demonstrate that this measure of robustness is consistent with the quantum states of the particles and their correlations. Finally, we examine the quantum state of the system when it is mixed with an equal amount of white noise, showing that it is possible to identify the presence of quantum correlations by observing the transitions between the boxes. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the quantum states of the three particles in this setup. In conclusion, we believe that a more comprehensive and detailed analysis of the quantum states of the three particles is necessary to fully understand the quantum mechanical nature of this quantum puzzle. After $|V|$ turns, both players own a set of vertices of equal size; an edge connects these sets in a new graph if it exists. The objective for each player is to maximize the degree of their respective set in this new graph, with Alice winning if her set achieves a higher degree. Lastly, the paper constructs a variety of belial algebras that are not free. To achieve this, the authors introduce the speciality index of an algebra, demonstrating that any subvariety of the belial variety is the principal speciality variety of an algebra whose speciality index is less than or equal to its cardinality. Consequently, any variety consisting solely of belial algebras that are not free must be the speciality variety of an algebra with a speciality index greater than or equal to its cardinality. Finally, it is proven that for any cardinal $\kappa > 2$, the principal speciality variety of a $\kappa$-belial algebra with speciality index $\kappa$ is a subvariety of the $\kappa$-belial variety. This result implies that the variety of $\kappa$-belial algebras is not the variety of subalgebras of the free $\kappa$-belial algebra on a countable set of generators. Moreover, for any cardinal $\kappa > 2$, a $\kappa$-belial algebra with speciality index $\kappa$ is constructed. It is also shown that for any cardinal $\kappa > 2$, a $\kappa$-belial algebra with speciality index $\kappa$ exists.

the scarcity of social graphs, which are essential for elucidating the social dynamics behind social media content. This paper introduces a novel method to reconstruct social graphs from Twitter data using user behavioral patterns. The approach employs a probabilistic model to estimate the social influence between users. We evaluated the method's efficacy in classifying tweets regarding the 2019 Chilean social movement and successfully applied it to forecast tweet categories with an accuracy of 71.42%. Furthermore, we utilized the technique to anticipate trending topics in Chile. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leandromgarcia/social-graph-reconstruction.

### 1. Introduction

#### 1.1. Social Media Analysis and the Need for Social Graphs

Social networks have become integral to contemporary life, facilitating communication and information dissemination. These platforms are frequently leveraged for sentiment analysis, opinion mining, and trend detection. However, most Twitter analysis techniques fail to account for social dynamics, a limitation that can be mitigated by incorporating social graphs. These graphs help reveal the relationships between users and their behaviors, offering deeper insights into how social connections influence online activity.

#### 1.2. The Challenge of Estimating Social Influence

Despite their value, social graphs are rarely available for Twitter analysis. Constructing these graphs is difficult because of Twitter's privacy settings, which restrict access to user connections. Consequently, researchers must rely on methods to estimate social influence. Various strategies exist for this estimation, including analyzing user behavior, examining retweeting patterns, and integrating both approaches. This study focuses on a method that estimates social influence by modeling user behaviors.

### 2. Methodology

#### 2.1. Estimating Influence from User Behaviors

This section outlines a method for estimating social influence derived from specific user behaviors. The approach is inspired by the work of Kwon et al. (2018), who modeled user behaviors to predict trending topics. Their work demonstrated that users with higher social influence are more likely to trigger a trend. Our study builds upon their methodology to estimate individual social influence.

#### 2.2. The Chilesocial 2019 Movement

Chilesocial 2019 refers to a series of protests in Chile sparked by the assassination of journalist Felipe González. These demonstrations garnered significant attention from Twitter users. We analyzed a subset of tweets from this movement to test the proposed user behavior model.

We demonstrate that for a specific class of channels, any initial correlation between the channel's input modes can be transformed into Wigner negativity in the output modes. This resulting negativity is proportional to the quantum mutual information present in the input, offering a quantitative measure of how much initial correlation is necessary to generate Wigner negativity under a channel's action. This relationship connects a gravitational model in an asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spacetime with a conformal field theory defined on its boundary. A key insight from this connection is that quantum fields can be defined through the eigenvalues of the Laplacian operator on the spacetime manifold. This study extends that concept to higher-spin fields by utilizing the eigenvalues of the spin-1/2 Dirac operator. This paper aims to investigate the color-magnitude slope within the framework of single stellar population (SSP) models, which are characterized by age and metallicity. We computed the V-I slope by calculating the magnitude difference between the cluster's blue end (extreme horizontal branch stars) and its main sequence tip. The resulting slope was then compared against empirical data. Our findings indicate a strong correlation between the V-I slope and metallicity, a relationship that aligns well with observed trends. Furthermore, we evaluated the utility of this slope as a metallicity indicator. Our results suggest that the slope is highly effective for determining metallicities in both Galactic globular clusters and extragalactic systems. Finally, we derived a new empirical relation between the V-I slope and metallicity, which aligns closely with theoretical predictions. This relation is applicable to stellar populations with ages exceeding 10 Gyr and spans a metallicity range from -0.6 to +0.1 dex. Additionally, we have developed a corresponding Python code to facilitate the calculation of metallicities using the V-I slope. This code is accessible at the following URL: http://www.astro.ufrgs.br/~josecarlos/Python_Code_V-I_Slope.html. The accuracy of the method is estimated at approximately 0.05 dex. In conclusion, the V-I slope represents a valuable tool for estimating the metallicities of old stellar populations. This is particularly significant for the external Galaxy, where metallicities are often uncertain, and for Galactic globular clusters, where it offers a complementary method to traditional approaches. The primary advantage of this technique lies in its simplicity, as it relies on the measurement of just two magnitudes. Future work will focus on refining the relation by incorporating stellar mass as an additional parameter. In this context, we will apply the method to a sample of Galactic globular clusters with known masses. Additionally, we intend to apply the method to a sample of dwarf galaxies with uncertain metallicities to compare our results with existing literature. This research examines a system consisting of $N$ particles with unequal sizes suspended in a liquid confined within a channel of sufficiently small width to block all particles from passing through. This theory is derived from the random walk theory of a particle in one dimension, incorporating the effects of particle size, channel width, and the exclusion principle. Furthermore, a relationship for the diffusion coefficient is suggested as a function of these same factors. The validity of this proposed theory and the resulting relationship for the diffusion coefficient are supported by the observed data. These outcomes are expected to aid in understanding the Brownian motion of particles in single file systems. Ultimately, this study may contribute to the development of nanotechnologies. where each player selects a strategy to optimize an objective function that depends not only on their own choice but also on the strategies of others. This interaction creates a complex challenge, particularly when players are "rational but not fully rational," meaning they possess limited computational resources. In such scenarios, the resulting dynamics are inherently complex, often defying simple analytical solutions. This paper introduces a novel method for exactly solving complex games by leveraging the self-dual polynomial method originally developed for finding perfect matchings in graphs. We demonstrate the method by exactly computing the Nash equilibrium in the "Battle of the Sexes" game under fully rational conditions and in the Median Voter model when players are completely rational. Furthermore, we derive the unique Nash equilibrium in the Median Voter model for fully rational but computationally constrained players. These findings are subsequently applied to analyze the Median Voter model featuring bounded rationality, offering a direct comparison with a recently proposed mean-field theory. Our results indicate a qualitative divergence from the mean-field approach, specifically revealing a phase transition in how equilibrium states depend on player rationality. Additionally, we identify a critical threshold for bounded rationality; below this threshold, the model exhibits a unique fully rational equilibrium, whereas above it, both a fully rational and a fully bounded rational equilibrium coexist. Finally, we examine the model's behavior as players approach full rationality, observing that the system undergoes a phase transition from a mean-field-like state to a fully rational equilibrium. This transition is characterized by a divergence in the second-order susceptibility, which aligns with the divergence of the mean-field theory at its own critical point, thereby establishing a direct link between the model's and the theory's critical points. This provides strong numerical evidence validating the mean-field theory. These findings are also extended to fully constrained versions of both the Median Voter and Hotelling models. Overall, these results represent the first application of the self-dual polynomial method to games. Beyond their theoretical significance, these exactly solvable models may serve as a foundation for developing quantum algorithms to efficiently compute Nash equilibria in games. This could enable the simulation of such simulations using near-term quantum computers, thereby exactly solving games that are provably intractable for classical computers. Finally, we outline a pathway for exactly solving general games by reducing them to finding perfect matchings in a specific type of graph. By applying this reduction to the Median Voter model, we confirm that computing the median voter's rationality threshold is NP-hard. Consequently, our exactly solvable Median Voter model serves as the first evidence that such a quantum algorithm

age spread within star-forming regions by pinpointing young stellar populations in the Perseus molecular cloud. **Methods.** We compiled a sample of 1,000 young stars with well-determined ages and distances, selected from the broader Perseus cloud collection. **Results.** Our analysis reveals that the stars in Perseus are not coeval; instead, they exhibit a significant age spread ranging from 0.5 to 10 Myr. This dispersion is primarily driven by the presence of stars with ages between 0.5 and 2.0 Myr, which are concentrated in the southern sector of the cloud. Conversely, stars older than 2.0 Myr are distributed more uniformly across the entire cloud. These findings suggest that star formation in Perseus occurred in multiple episodes, with the most recent activity centered in the southern sector. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stars in Perseus can be categorized into two distinct groups based on their ages and distances: (1) a young population aged 0.5–2.0 Myr, located south of the $\lambda$ Perseus association, and (2) an intermediate-aged population older than 2.0 Myr, found throughout the cloud. The younger group is associated with the $\lambda$ Perseus and IC 348 star-forming regions, while the older group is linked to Chamaeleon I, $\chi$ Ophiuchus, and Taurus. These results align with the hypothesis that the stars in Perseus originated from different parent molecular clouds. **Conclusions.** Our findings suggest that the age spread in star-forming regions is substantial and that the stars therein do not share a common age. These insights may aid in understanding the mechanisms driving star formation. Additionally, we have created a website hosting the data and analysis presented in this study. The site includes a tool that allows users to input stellar parameters to determine membership in Perseus and identify the most probable age range for each star. Given that traditional speech synthesisers often struggle to generate speech at fundamental frequencies distinct from their training data, we developed a neural network conditioned on fundamental frequency to address this limitation. While prior research has utilized deep learning for speech emulation, our work represents the first application of this technology to speech emulation tasks. We trained a conditional neural network to learn a mapping from a source fundamental frequency to a target one, using speech as the intermediary. The training dataset comprises natural speech from various speakers, each paired with multiple examples of the same phonemes spoken at different fundamental frequencies. Our findings indicate that the network successfully learns this mapping, resulting in both speech and emotional emulation. Furthermore, the emitted speech retains the acoustic characteristics of the original speaker. The source fundamental frequency is supplied as a Mel-frequency cepstrum coefficient vector, and the network produces both spectral and excitation parameters. The source fundamental frequency can be any value within a broad range, provided it falls within approximately 10 semitones of the training set's frequency range. The source speaker is determined by the phonemes in the target utterance and the fundamental frequency of the source utterance. Finally, the network's outputs are converted back into audio using a neural network-based source-filter separation algorithm. These observables may possess discontinuities, yet we establish decay in Hölder norms provided they are quasicontinuous, meaning their total variation remains bounded away from infinity. This approach extends previous findings by Baladi and Saied (2019) regarding smooth observables in uniformly expanding Anosov semiflows to include certain rough observables in Anosov flows and diffusive observables in Brownian motion. Furthermore, we apply this result to establish exponential decay of correlations for uniformly expanding semiflows containing quasicontinuous observables. This application depends on the specific structure of the transfer operator and its relationship with the spectral gap of the nontransfer operator, distinguishing it from the decay of Hölder norms. Our strategy avoids the intricate analysis of branch points and the pullback technique, which are typically required when dealing with discontinuous observables. Instead, this methodology is anticipated to apply more readily to uniformly expanding and diffusive systems. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this strategy by proving exponential decay of correlations for a specific class of discontinuous observables in nonuniformly expanding Brownian motion. This achievement addresses a limitation in the original work by Denker and Urbański (2009), which only demonstrated decay for continuous observables. Additionally, this work addresses a question posed by Denker and Steif in 2018. In a separate section, we apply these quasicontinuity results to a broad class of continuous observables in uniformly expanding Brownian motion that possess a finite number of discontinuities and possess bounded total variation. This class encompasses observables with a finite number of jump discontinuities where both left and right limits are finite, as well as those with a finite number of removable discontinuities. This finding addresses a specific issue raised by Baladi and Saied in 2019. We begin by defining a weighted space of observables to demonstrate that the transfer operator maps into the space of bounded observables equipped with a specific weighted norm. Subsequently, we apply this result to Brownian motion, demonstrating that the transfer operator acts boundedly on the space of continuous observables under a certain weighted norm, thereby implying exponential decay of correlations for a wide class of observables that are not necessarily quasicontinuous. This study examines the entanglement between two photons generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, which is driven by the quantum fluctuations of the pump laser. We demonstrate that the pump laser's quantum properties are directly reflected in the state of the entangled photon pairs. Specifically, the squeezing of the photon pairs is shown to be equal to the sub-shot-noise intensity fluctuations of the pairs and is derived from the pump laser's quantum properties. Furthermore, we establish a method to verify the quantum nature of the pump laser using entangled photon pairs. The findings in this research have significant implications for quantum metrology and quantum information technology. Additionally, this work introduces a novel approach for characterizing quantum light based on entangled photon pairs, which could serve as a valuable resource for future quantum information applications. The experimental setup for measuring the quantum properties of the pump laser with high efficiency is shown to be simple and robust. These results can be extended to scenarios where the pump laser is a two-mode squeezed vacuum, which is also a quantum resource. Consequently, this research offers a new perspective for utilizing quantum light in quantum metrology and information technology. Finally, the study demonstrates that entangled photon pairs can function as a probe to examine the quantum properties of the pump laser. A review is provided covering the inflationary epoch, the subsequent reheating phase that enabled inflation to be observable, and the formation of primordial density perturbations. An analysis is conducted on how these density fluctuations are influenced by the inflationary potential, including their amplitude and the scaling of their scale invariance. Finally, the consequences of these fluctuations on the observable universe are explored, specifically how they generate temperature and polarization anisotropies in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and induce large-scale structure in the present day. These observations allow for the derivation of constraints on the inflationary potential. Finally, inflation is tested against CMB data and large-scale observations, and a selection of inflationary models is evaluated in light of current data. This testing process also identifies a necessary lower bound for the number of e-folds of inflation. The conclusion addresses the end of inflation and the transition to the hot Big Bang, as well as the current status of the inflationary paradigm. Lastly, it discusses the potential for discovering new physics through CMB and large-scale observations, particularly regarding the scale of the reheating temperature. To assess the validity of this result, we employ a machine learning approach to determine the pole mass of the $W$ boson directly from experimental data. Our method utilizes the data set from CDF II, specifically the distribution of the missing transverse momentum relative to the missing transverse momentum angle. We determine the pole mass to be $M_W^{pole} = 80.42 \pm 0.12$ GeV, a value consistent with both the Standard Model and the recent PDG average. Furthermore, we examine the impact of theoretical assumptions on the mass determination by analyzing the effects of varying the jet energy scale and the number of jets within the event. These studies are conducted using Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we compare our findings with other recent $W$ boson mass measurements. Our results suggest that the significant discrepancy observed in the transverse mass distribution might stem from the treatment of jet parton shower splittings. Additionally, we note that the choice of jet algorithm can introduce substantial variations in the final outcome. We also investigate the potential influence of parton shower modeling on the mass determination by testing different particle shower programs. Finally, we address the challenges associated with applying this analysis to future experimental data. In conclusion, we propose that the recent $W$ boson mass measurement discrepancy may arise from the specific data set used and the treatment of jet parton shower splittings. We further recommend that upcoming experiments should incorporate a comprehensive analysis of systematic uncertainties to ensure reliable mass determinations. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the complete set of free states and free transformations, characterized by the closure of the state space under these interactions. Consequently, we derive the necessary mathematical tools to analyze and quantify the information content of both free and non-free resources. As an initial application, we demonstrate that any state of a single qubit or system of $n$ qubits decomposes into a mixture of "extremal" resources, which are mutually unreachable and define the boundaries of non-free resource transformations. The primary motivation is that information metrics are essential for defining the geometry of statistical manifolds, a concept deeply integrated into both statistical inference and machine learning. A prominent example is Amari's information geometry, which employs a specific statistical connection and information geometry derived from the Fisher information metric. In this framework, a two-dimensional statistical manifold corresponds to the torus, representing a two-dimensional time series. We demonstrate that the information geometry of the torus can be fully characterized by a single scalar value, $\alpha$, which quantifies the geometric properties of the statistical manifold. This paper presents a method to estimate $\alpha$ from data using the information kernel. Furthermore, we evaluate this estimator through numerical simulations and apply it to analyze the statistical manifolds of actual data. The results indicate that this approach is effective for estimating the geometry of statistical manifolds. Additionally, we find that the Fisher information metric of a two-dimensional time series tends to exhibit non-Euclidean characteristics. Finally, we propose a novel hypothesis test for the statistical manifold based on $\alpha$. This test operates under the null hypothesis that the statistical manifold is locally Euclidean, offering a new perspective on statistical inference for time series. low-density parity-check codes (LDPC) where any two columns in the parity-check matrix share at most one 1, and any three columns share at most two 1s. The rate of these codes scales as $1 - \frac{2\log_2{t} + 2}{n}$, where $t$ denotes the number of points in a projective plane of order $n-2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that codes from this family achieve the LDPC threshold theorem, meaning they can be simulated by local Hamiltonians with an extremely small ground-state energy gap. This finding indicates that quantum LDPC codes are likely susceptible to noise-induced leakage from the logical code space. Consequently, our results provide additional evidence that identifying quantum LDPC codes with large energy gaps remains a challenging problem. Finally, we conjecture that LDPC codes possessing both a high rate and a large minimum distance—properties that would make them valuable for fault-tolerant quantum computing—may similarly exhibit a tiny energy gap. Specifically, we propose a family of quantum LDPC codes where the distance $d$ and block size $n$ satisfy $d = \Omega(n^{1/2})$, with a rate of $1 - \frac{2\log_2{d} + 2}{n}$. For any constant $t$, we exhibit a set of $k$-local Hamiltonians with a ground-state energy gap of at most $n^{-t}$. These results are derived from a family of quantum LDPC codes constructed using a specific set of combinatorial objects known as Steiner systems. In the final section, we demonstrate that the ability to embed such systems into a Hamiltonian can be generalized to a broader class of embedding problems, which we term "quantum embedding problems." We believe this framework will be a useful tool for future research. In summary, our work demonstrates that it is feasible to construct quantum LDPC codes with highly small energy gaps, thereby suggesting that the challenge of designing quantum LDPC codes with large energy gaps is equally formidable. This insight may guide the search for practical quantum LDPC codes suitable for near-term quantum computing applications. Our findings also have implications for the theoretical study of quantum error-correcting codes. We anticipate that this paper will aid in the development of quantum LDPC codes with large energy gaps, a critical requirement for their practical implementation. Additionally, our results may contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between quantum error-correcting codes and quantum many-body Hamiltonians. We

Specifically, we examine a disordered Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model featuring long-range hopping, where the bulk topology remains robust against disorder, yet the corresponding boundary mode is highly sensitive to disordered potential. Our numerical findings reveal that the probability distribution of the largest hopping matrix elements in the bulk exhibits a universal double-peak structure. We demonstrate that the single-peak among these two shifts with increasing disorder, while the other remains relatively stable. By analyzing the eigenvalue distribution of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, we show that the peak position of the spectrum near the origin serves as an effective order parameter for topological phases in the disordered context. Additionally, we investigate the finite-size effects associated with these bulk properties and evaluate their utility in detecting the topological phase transition. Finally, we extend these concepts to more complex disordered systems, including the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with complex hopping and a non-Hermitian generalized Kitaev model with long-range hopping. These findings highlight the significance of investigating bulk-boundary correspondence in disordered environments and suggest that bulk properties can effectively characterize topological phases even when boundary properties fail to do so due to disorder. This approach offers a new perspective for exploring disorder effects in topological insulators. Our analysis also holds potential for experimental verification within non-Hermitian photonic systems. Our empirical analysis of 24 games from the dynamic CH literature reveals a distribution of play depths that deviates from both the static and dynamic CH predictions. While the static model anticipates a concentration on its second depth, the dynamic model forecasts no such focal point. This finding supports the dynamic CH model's core assertion: as players adapt their depth over time, they tend to increase it until they surpass the Nash depth threshold. Finally, we examine how the set of games influences play depth, demonstrating that players in low-payoff games are more likely to exceed the CH second depth, whereas high-payoff games drive depths below this threshold. These patterns align with the theoretical property that higher payoffs encourage greater depth. Overall, these results bolster the dynamic CH model's claim that players with varying depths are motivated by payoff maximization. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings for the evolution of player sophistication. Finally, we propose and analyze a new class of games—the beauty contest with continuous payoffs—where the payoff function is defined by a polynomial of the average guess raised to an unknown power $m$. Experimental findings suggest that $m$ exceeds 1, indicating that participants in this beauty contest game are generally sophisticated. Our results indicate that as $m$ increases, play depth rises, though the relationship is not strictly monotonic. These outcomes are consistent with the dynamic CH model's prediction regarding the impact of the payoff function on play depth. Finally, we demonstrate that the dynamic CH model is applicable to continuous beauty contest games. In these scenarios, the second depth is typically below 2, implying that only first-level players (best responders) should be eliminated in the iteration process. This conclusion aligns with our empirical findings. In summary, these results provide strong evidence for the dynamic CH model as an effective framework for understanding behavior in this class of games. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending the dynamic CH model to continuous games. The game unfolds over multiple rounds, alternating between day and night phases. During the day, the active faction discusses their strategy, while the night allows the opposing faction to execute actions such as eliminating or gathering information. oscale conductive particles is governed by percolation, a process where adding filler to a matrix establishes a system-wide electrical pathway. Although the mean-field percolation threshold for spherical particles is widely accepted as 16%, the true percolation limit for nanoparticles is likely lower due to the influence of van der Waals forces. This study demonstrates that van der Waals forces cause particles to adhere and deform at distances significantly beyond their immediate neighbors, resulting in a percolation threshold of just 0.4% in a bulk system. Furthermore, these forces induce nanoparticle deformation prior to percolation, which significantly enhances percolation near the threshold volume fraction. We validate this theoretical prediction using both numerical simulations and experimental data from gold nanoparticle percolation. Our findings indicate that percolation can be achieved with nanoparticle fillers at volume fractions approximately 40 times lower than previously thought possible. Additionally, we show that the mean free path of electrons traveling between nanoparticles is only a few times larger than the particle diameter, a scale that is optimal for designing high-performance thermoelectric materials. These insights into the mechanics of percolation and nanoparticle deformation offer a foundation for developing new technologies utilizing nanoparticle composites. This paper examines the learning dynamics of a single-layer MoE with sparsity under stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We demonstrate that sparsity accelerates convergence by reducing interference among experts, resulting in distinct convergence rates for sparse versus dense scenarios. This analysis reveals that a cosmological constant induces a non-trivial coupling between spacetime and matter fields. Specifically, this interaction causes local causal structure and matter fields to influence one another, even in the absence of dynamical coupling. Furthermore, this interaction may fundamentally alter the continuum limit of space-time and fields at the quantum level, potentially giving rise to a conserved quantity in quantum gravity. Finally, we demonstrate that this interaction is likely of non-perturbative nature, implying that conclusions drawn from effective field theory calculations in the presence of a cosmological constant might be unreliable. These insights have broad implications for numerous cosmological and particle physics phenomena. We also examine this interaction within Hořava-Lifshitz gravity, a non-perturbative theory of quantum gravity. Finally, we explore the implications of this interaction for the global symmetries arising from higher-form gauge theories. We show that these symmetries can be locally restored by employing a non-abelian 2-form gauge field, and we present evidence that this construction is robust against quantum gravitational effects. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of these findings. These controls possess the characteristic that their closures are invariant under the associated control flows, yet they are not necessarily closed or convex. We demonstrate that optimal controls for such a map can exhibit discontinuities along specific hyperplanes within the control space, a phenomenon that occurs because the closure of the control set may fail to be weakly invariant. Furthermore, we establish that weakly invariant valued controls constitute the largest collection of controls for which the following property holds: if a control is present, then every control within its closure is also admissible. This characteristic is particularly significant for analyzing the stability of optimality. Additionally, we provide an example of a map where the largest control set is weakly invariant but lacks convexity. Finally, we present several illustrative examples of discontinuities in optimal controls, including cases involving weakly invariant control sets. These examples illustrate that, generally, optimal controls are merely measurable functions, even when the control sets are closed and convex. However, we also present a sufficient condition ensuring that optimal controls are continuous whenever the controls belong to the closure of the control set. This condition imposes a constraint on the continuity of the boundary of the control sets. Such continuity is crucial for investigating stability issues in optimal controls. Specifically, it ensures that a control set remains admissible upon slight perturbations of its boundary. Consequently, we can demonstrate that under appropriate conditions, there exist neighborhoods in the space of closed sets such that any control within a control set and its neighborhood remains admissible. This property is essential for studying the stability of optimality. We also present an example demonstrating that optimal controls can be discontinuous precisely when appropriate conditions on the continuity of the boundary of the control set are violated. In this scenario, a control set becomes admissible only when perturbed to a sufficient degree. Finally, we present an example of optimal controls where the control set is admissible only under a sufficiently large perturbation. The proposed approach involves training the network on data augmented with diverse transformations, followed by the sequential removal of specific augmentation types. This iterative process continues until an optimal configuration is reached, defined as the point where further extraction yields no additional performance gains. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating improved outcomes on two datasets: MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Consequently, the proposed method offers a promising avenue for future studies in data-limited environments. Furthermore, the code and experiments are made available on GitHub to support the reproducibility of results. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/ahmed-eldin/Deep-Transfer-Learning.

This study examines how social networks influence the adoption of social norms and the proliferation of innovations. We introduce a unified stochastic framework that integrates information diffusion with various mechanisms for changing social norms and adopting innovations. Specifically, we analyze a unified random process that merges the well-known Independent Cascade (IC) and Linear Threshold (LT) models. Within this framework, nodes adopt an action based on a random combination of the IC and LT models, where the mixing parameter follows a Beta distribution. This approach yields two significant outcomes: first, it enables the simultaneous investigation of social network impacts on both social norm adoption and innovation uptake; and second, it provides a unified method for comparing and contrasting the behaviors of the IC and LT models. Furthermore, we derive the closed-form solution for the spreading process and demonstrate that it allows for the calculation of the spreading curve and the expected number of activated nodes as a function of the initial seed set. Finally, we apply our framework to investigate the dynamics of social norm formation and innovation adoption across diverse network topologies. In a scenario involving a social norm that rewards cooperative nodes, we observe that networks with a higher LT proportion exhibit greater resistance to norm-breaking behaviors. Conversely, in scenarios where an innovation competes with an outdated one, we find that nodes with more incoming edges are more likely to adopt the new innovation. These findings are supported by extensive simulations. Our results offer valuable insights for future research on the dynamics of social norm formation, social pressure, and the adoption of innovations and rumors. The proposed unified framework serves as a versatile tool for analyzing the complex interplay between social network structures and the diffusion of various information types. Our future work will focus on extending this framework to incorporate node heterogeneity and dynamic network topologies. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/zhaoxiaofeng/Unified-IC-LT-Model}. This dark sector is initialized in a symmetric vacuum and features a characteristic scale for its first excited state. We examine two distinct mechanisms for vacuum transition between these states. The first involves a small perturbation of the dark sector by a new, very heavy particle. These concepts are illustrated through a practical case study involving the integration of RDF data from DBpedia and Wikidata. The study is motivated by the objective of constructing a canonical graph from specific named classes to facilitate a global comparison of properties associated with those classes in both datasets. Our approach involves mapping source relations to RDF terms and identifying RDF properties that function as surjective mappings, while also proposing a method to convert generated data into resources. Furthermore, we analyze the complexity of full and tgd repairs in data exchange scenarios. Our findings indicate that while the existence and uniqueness of full repairs and universal graph cover are decidable, the same cannot be said for tgd repairs and graph cover under a subset of these dependencies. To address this, we introduce a new dependency class, RAC, which allows for the characterization of solutions and graph cover for this specific subset. Finally, we establish the undecidability of graph cover for general data exchange scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion on the results and potential directions for future research. While deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance, they often require extensive training data, which hinders their effectiveness for low-resource languages. \section{Introduction}

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is a critical component of numerous applications, including Virtual Assistants (VAs) and Voice User Interfaces (VUIs). ASR systems are typically developed using deep learning techniques, which have become the standard approach for such systems. However, deep learning models are data-intensive, necessitating large volumes of labeled data to train high-performing models. Acquiring such large datasets is often difficult and costly, particularly for low-resource languages. Consequently, transfer learning has become a widely adopted solution, enabling the reuse of knowledge from related tasks or domains to improve model performance with less labeled data. This paper evaluates two specific transfer learning strategies for ASR: cross-task and cross-domain adaptation. Cross-task transfer involves adapting a model trained on one task to a different but related task, whereas cross-domain transfer adapts a model from one domain to a different one within the same task. The evaluation leverages data from Microsoft Assistant Development Kits (ADK), a framework that provides pre-trained ASR models and other functionalities for VAs. The findings demonstrate the benefits of transfer learning in improving the accuracy of deep learning-based ASR models, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. The results also highlight the importance of carefully selecting source and target domains and tasks during the transfer process. Furthermore, the study identifies key challenges and opportunities for future research in this area. Finally,

This study aims to determine the initial mass and evolutionary history of a Be star by analyzing the chemical composition of its stellar wind. We employed the 3D-1D method, combining 3D stellar atmosphere models with 1D stellar wind models. The 1D wind model incorporates a variable mass-loss rate and a non-uniform density distribution, accounting for the wind's rotation and the presence of spiral structures. Chemical abundances were calculated using the MESA code, and the resulting spectra were compared with observed data. By utilizing 3D atmospheric models, we derived the effective temperature and surface gravity for Be star HD 161091, finding values of 13,000 K and 1.95, respectively. The 1D wind model was adjusted to match the observed H$\alpha$ emission line, yielding a mass-loss rate of $1.1 \times 10^{-7} M_{\odot} \text{ yr}^{-1}$. The spectrum synthesis successfully reproduced the observed spectral features, including the H$\alpha$ emission line, Fe I absorption lines, and the Fe II 3720-21 doublet. The derived photospheric abundances for C, N, O, and He align with solar values, while Fe is approximately 0.5 dex below solar levels. These findings suggest that HD 161091 is likely the remnant core of an AGB star. Furthermore, the observed photospheric abundances indicate that the progenitor AGB star had an initial mass of approximately 10 $M_{\odot}$. This result supports the AGB channel as the primary formation mechanism for Be stars. Additionally, the rotationally modified mixing-length theory (MLM) in MESA was found to be essential for accurately simulating the AGB phase. Finally, the observed wind mass-loss rate is consistent with the 1998 study by Vink et al., which established a relationship between wind mass loss and stellar mass. of quantum mechanics (Q.M.) suggests that measurement results are predetermined by the complete state of the universe at an initial time, prior to any measurements. This approach posits that while individual outcomes are random, the statistical predictions of Q.M. are accurately reproduced. The authors of the proposed paper argue that this interpretation is untenable because the superdeterministic framework required to enable interactions that yield Q.M. predictions contradicts the probabilistic nature of Q.M. itself, which governs the universe's evolution. Consequently, the paper aims to demonstrate that the specific superdeterministic structure necessary to reproduce Q.M. predictions is itself unable to occur within a universe governed by Q.M. Therefore, the second part of the proposal—demonstrating how to reconcile Q.M. predictions with Bell's theorem—must also be examined. To achieve this, the paper will outline the fundamental components of superdeterminism, discuss the free will assumption, and analyze the second part of the proposal. Ultimately, it will illustrate that the probabilistic nature of Q.M. and the absence of long-range correlations in space and time are incompatible with the necessary superdeterministic structure. Furthermore, it will clarify that the theorem referenced in the title is a specific instance of a more general theorem applicable to any quantum process. Finally, the paper will address the misconception that this theorem constitutes a contradiction in nature, demonstrating that it can be resolved without sacrificing the probabilistic nature of Q.M. or the validity of Q.M. predictions. Finally, the paper will examine the implications of superdeterminism for metaphysics, specifically regarding the nature of time, causality, and the origin of the universe. It will also explore the link between superdeterminism and the Big Bounce cosmological model, which posits that the universe originated from a previous contracting phase. Finally, the paper will address the argument that superdeterminism is incompatible with the Second Law of Thermodynamics, which states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases over time. It will demonstrate that this argument fails because the probabilistic nature of Q.M. is essential for explaining the increase in entropy in our universe. Furthermore, the paper will show that the probabilistic nature of Q.M. is not merely compatible with superdeterminism but is actually necessary for it. Consequently, both the proof of Bell's theorem and Q.M. must be understood within a quantum cosmological framework. Finally, the paper will address the issue of how to select the correct interpretation of Q.M. among various options

Wilsonian effective action for lattice Yang-Mills theory to derive the renormalization group flow equations. Our methodology diverges from recent lattice constructions of continuum renormalization group flows, which are derived from the lattice partition function. Instead, we directly analyze the evolution of the lattice effective action itself. This approach yields a single first-order differential equation for the dependence of the effective coupling on the lattice cutoff. Furthermore, this equation can be solved exactly. Consequently, we obtain a complete and explicit formula for the running coupling that applies to any scheme, regardless of its renormalization conditions. Finally, we examine the implications of these results within the functional renormalization group framework. In this context, the differential equation governing the coupling evolution is equivalent to the non-local functional differential equation previously proposed. Additionally, the running coupling derived here satisfies the non-local consistency condition established in prior work. These findings are intended to facilitate a more rigorous and comprehensive investigation of the functional renormalization group method. Notably, the explicit expression for the running coupling may also prove valuable in other scenarios, such as the large-N limit of Yang-Mills theory. Such an explicit form could facilitate more direct and less ambiguous assessments of infrared and ultraviolet fixed points, as well as the associated critical exponents. This utility extends beyond Yang-Mills theory to other gauge theories, including QCD, as well as non-perturbative renormalization group approaches like the ANMC method. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of our results with those from the conventional ANMC method. Our findings indicate that the ANMC approach, in its standard perturbative form, fails to accurately capture the non-perturbative infrared behavior of Yang-Mills theory. However, by utilizing the exact formula for the running coupling in an ANMC-style approach, we can successfully reproduce the infrared behavior of Yang-Mills theory. This suggests that the apparent failure of ANMC in its standard perturbative form may stem from the unphysical nature of the approximations employed. Specifically, the ANMC approach appears to be fundamentally compatible with non-abelian infrared behavior, provided that the running of the coupling constant is handled correctly. These conclusions are supported by numerical evidence from recent studies on Yang-Mills theory in the large-N limit. Our results suggest that the Wilsonian functional renormalization group method, when rigorously applied, may yield a complete non-perturbative description of the infrared behavior of Yang-Mills theory. This could potentially offer new insights into the confinement mechanism in non-abelian gauge theories.

detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a general-purpose instrument designed to measure the properties of particles generated in high-energy collisions. Given the intense rate of events recorded during LHC operations, the CMS data acquisition system must rapidly filter and record only a small fraction of these collisions for offline analysis. This presentation will detail the performance of the system during Run 2 (2015–2018) and its anticipated capabilities for the upcoming high-luminosity phase, which will operate at significantly increased event rates. The LHC currently delivers proton-proton collision data to the CMS experiment at a rate of approximately 100 MHz, with each collision record, or "event," containing roughly 1000 parameters. Due to the overwhelming volume of data, the data acquisition system is tasked with selecting and storing only about 1000 events per second. Additionally, the presentation will outline the transition to the data-taking phase for Run 3, which is scheduled to commence in late 2021. This phase will operate the detector at significantly higher luminosity, leading to increased event rates and necessitating further enhancements to both hardware and software trigger systems. Finally, the talk will highlight the new features introduced during Run 3 and their expected performance under the elevated luminosity conditions.

The objective is to create a deterministic, data-driven evolution model capable of forecasting turbulent flow dynamics across arbitrary spatial domains and various flow regimes. This study presents a method to rapidly and accurately determine the quantum processes of arbitrary multi-qubit systems by leveraging the symmetries of the Pauli group. The approach utilizes a stabilizer circuit to achieve the necessary measurements, and the Pauli expansion coefficients of the quantum process are derived through the application of the inclusion-exclusion principle. The method's accuracy and speed are validated across various scenarios, including single- and two-qubit processes involving both Clifford and non-Clifford gates. Furthermore, the technique is extended to handle redundant processes and scenarios with incomplete gate sets. Tomographic data for a three-qubit system featuring a combination of single and two-qubit gates is also provided. Overall, the findings indicate that this method is highly effective for the fast and precise characterization of arbitrary multi-qubit quantum processes. It is anticipated that the inclusion-exclusion principle will serve as a valuable tool for the continued advancement of quantum process tomography. We introduce a variant of mean curvature known as the relative mean curvature, defined as the standard mean curvature minus the constant value of the mean curvature on the boundary. We demonstrate that the Cheeger constant can be bounded by this relative mean curvature. These findings have significant implications for spectral geometry, particularly in analyzing the first non-trivial Neumann eigenvalue of the Laplacian on domains with mean curvature flow. This sensitivity is frequently enhanced through optimal interrogation times and the utilization of quantum correlations, such as those found in entangled states like the N-qubit GHZ state. However, these optimizations introduce specific limitations and trade-offs. In this study, we demonstrate that further sensitivity improvements are achievable via a combined approach involving both optimal time estimation and quantum correlations. Notably, a modest correlation component within the N-qubit state suffices to reach the same level of sensitivity. Crucially, this strategy mitigates several trade-offs associated with GHZ measurements, including excessive decoherence impacts and the necessity for precise time optimization. Our findings indicate that the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for N-qubit Ramsey measurements utilizing an optimized time estimation protocol scales with the square of the number of qubits under conditions of weak decoherence. Furthermore, under strong decoherence, the QFI increases linearly with the number of qubits when using W-state correlations, a significant improvement over the zero-qubit correlation case. These results highlight the potential of optimal time estimation as a practical method for enhancing quantum phase measurement sensitivity. Additionally, we have developed a computational tool to calculate the QFI for N-qubit Ramsey measurements with optimized time estimation, which is available at https://github.com/zhaojiajun/Quantum-Fisher-Information-For-N-qubit-Ramsey-Measurement. This resource can facilitate a deeper understanding of the advantages and trade-offs of optimal time estimation in quantum phase measurements, thereby aiding future experimental designs. Finally, we discuss the practical feasibility of implementing optimal time estimation in current Ramsey measurement experiments. These conclusions are derived from a detailed analysis of quantum Fisher information, which forms the theoretical basis for quantum phase measurement sensitivity. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the N-qubit Ramsey measurement model and the concept of quantum Fisher information; Section 3 presents our findings on the advantages and trade-offs of optimal time estimation in quantum phase measurements, including a discussion on the practical feasibility in existing experiments; and Section 4 offers our concluding remarks. In the Appendix, we provide a discussion on the computational complexity of calculating the quantum Fisher information for N-qubit Ramsey measurements. While many existing methods rely on the structure of the underlying undirected graph, centrality in directed networks demands different approaches. This study examines directed centrality metrics through the lens of structural symmetry, a concept introduced in our prior research [1]. We establish the theoretical upper and lower bounds for multiple centrality types, including in-degree, out-degree, expected path length, expected shortest path length, average path length, shortest path distance, and average shortest path distance. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between the proposed structural symmetry and these directed centrality metrics. Finally, an experimental analysis is conducted on both synthetic and real-world directed networks to validate the derived properties and bounds. The findings indicate that nodes exhibiting higher structural symmetry tend to possess lower values for most directed centrality measures. Consequently, nodes with minimal structural symmetry are expected to have higher in-degree and out-degree, as well as lower average path lengths for both expected and average shortest paths relative to the source and target nodes. Additionally, these nodes with low structural symmetry are situated further away from one another in terms of shortest path distance. The results suggest that structural symmetry serves as a valuable metric for quantifying a node's structural importance in purely directed graphs. Furthermore, nodes with low structural symmetry are more likely to function as critical components within information systems.

We derive a solution that can be interpreted as a "weak" or linearized version of the Einstein field equation. We demonstrate that this solution yields a circular orbit without requiring the assumption of ad hoc postulates regarding the existence of attractive forces. Consequently, we argue that the weak gravitational field generated by a rotating massive ring can sustain a test mass in orbit at a distance equal to the ring's radius and moving at the same tangential speed. These bundles possess notable features, including an abstract representation via the determinant polynomial and the concept of a universal member, which is an pencil bundle containing all members under strict equivalence. The distance from a generic member to the bundle's boundary is characterized by the minimal index; however, when the minimal index is maximal (equal to n), the distance is determined instead by a specific invariant related to the characteristic polynomial. The paper investigates the structure of matrix pencil bundles under strict equivalence, with a primary focus on the 2x2 case. Additionally, the study examines the structure of regular bundles through the lens of the classical theory of linear differential equations. Finally, the problem of minimal realization for bundles of 2x2 pencils is addressed. The work concludes with an algorithm for finding the universal member and addresses the issue of continuous deformation within bundles under strict equivalence.

(MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in engineering and operations research, yet their resolution is challenging due to the discrete nature of variables and the complex relationships between objectives and decisions. This difficulty is amplified when dealing with non-convex objectives, which are common in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a hybrid algorithm that integrates multi-criteria branch-and-bound (MCBB) with evolutionary multi-objective optimization (EMO). The algorithm utilizes EMO to identify a subset of promising solutions that balance all objectives, feeding these into the branching strategy to narrow the search space. The process repeats until a termination condition is met, after which MCBB explores the remaining search space. This methodology is applied to a case study of a multi-material hot-metal vacuum arc remelting (MMHVAR) process. The results demonstrate that the algorithm is effective and that the final solution set covers the entire Pareto front, offering diverse and high-quality solutions. Additionally, the study confirms that the proposed algorithm is more efficient than standard EMO approaches. Finally, the paper advocates for the application of this method to MO-MINLP problems characterized by a small number of objectives and variables. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyao1996/MCBBEMO. The theory of black Lie groupoids, introduced in our prior work, provides a straightforward and robust method for addressing these generalized problems. Our framework simplifies the analysis of standard issues in this context and achieves this with a more efficient and conceptually clearer technical approach. umpy wind accretion model posits that the wind is not uniform but consists of dense clumps separated by voids. This scenario predicts that wind accretion will be interrupted by periods of low or negligible accretion when the compact object passes through these voids. Consequently, the X-ray flux should fluctuate between intervals of steady wind accretion and phases of significantly reduced or halted accretion. This paper introduces a novel statistical method designed to identify such wind clumping signatures in the X-ray light curves of high-mass systems. The algorithm detects pairs of "on" and "off" states that align with the expected on-off-on pattern, accounting for potential gaps between the on-off and off-on transitions. Applied to the light curves of Cyg X-1, HDE 2295, and 4U 1543-47, the analysis found no evidence supporting wind clumping. These results are consistent with models of smooth, steady winds, although the sample size limitations prevent a definitive exclusion of clumping models. Furthermore, the algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations, confirming its ability to uncover on-off-on patterns even when on-off or off-on pairs occur independently. The findings indicate that this approach is particularly well-suited for analyzing long, continuous light curves. Finally, the study suggests that wind clumping may be more prevalent in supergiant donors compared to other types of high-mass X-ray binary systems. These results will be presented at the 47th International Astronomical Union General Assembly. [Abridged]

to assign compact labels to the vertices of a graph $G$ such that the edges traversing them provide a coarse approximation of their relative positions. This labeling must withstand the failure of a subset of vertices, ensuring that the labels remaining for the survivors still offer spatial proximity data. A prevalent model in ad-hoc wireless networks, where nodes communicate via unreliable, energy-limited, and bandwidth-constrained links, is the hop-hop metric labeling model. In this model, a label is associated with each vertex, and an edge label is formed by concatenating the labels of its endpoints; this label must reflect the vertex's hop distance from its incident edges.

In this paper, we introduce an algorithmic method for constructing fault-tolerant fault-tolerant (FTFT) labeling for trees. Given a tree $T$ with a root $r$, our approach combines port labeling with path labeling to achieve FTFT labeling with a stretch of $O(\log n)$. This solution is optimal, as we demonstrate a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ for FTFT tree labeling. Additionally, we present a FTFT labeling scheme for graphs with treewidth $t$ that attains a stretch of $O(t \log n)$.

Our algorithm is straightforward and relies on the observation that an FTFT labeling scheme can be derived from a standard labeling scheme. We also provide a labeling scheme for graphs with treewidth $t$ that incorporates port information. This scheme is derived from an existing path labeling scheme and is optimal regarding both stretch and label size. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this FTFT path labeling scheme can be converted into one without port information while maintaining the same stretch. This conversion is significant because path labeling schemes without port information are more widely recognized and easier to implement.

Finally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(t/\log t)$ for the size of path labeling schemes with port information, thereby proving that this optimal FTFT labeling scheme is also optimal in terms of label size. This result is optimal up to a logarithmic factor, as it matches the lower bound established by Chan et al. (2019) for path labeling schemes that do not utilize port information. This finding is surprising because it is well-known that including port information can reduce the size of path labeling schemes. This surprising result is specific to the fault-tolerant context, as it does not hold for non-FTFT path labeling schemes.
